questions.q: Which three types of objects does Azure Key Vault store?
options: Keys, secrets, and certificates
Only encryption keys, nothing else
Virtual machines, storage accounts, and networks
IAM roles, policies, and groups
questions.explain: Key Vault stores three distinct object types: keys (for encrypt/decrypt and sign/verify), secrets (arbitrary blobs like connection strings or passwords), and certificates (X.509, with renewal handling).

questions.q: What is the key difference between Key Vault's legacy access policies and Azure RBAC for Key Vault?
options: Access policies are faster but less secure than RBAC
RBAC can only be used with certificates, not keys or secrets
Access policies are a flat, vault-scoped permission list not governed by Azure role assignments, while RBAC for Key Vault uses standard Azure role assignments that show up in access reviews
There is no real difference; they are two names for the same mechanism
questions.explain: Access policies are the original vault-scoped model, invisible to Azure RBAC access reviews. Azure RBAC for Key Vault is the current recommended model, using standard role assignments scoped like any other Azure resource.

questions.q: For a principal to actually use an AWS KMS key, what has to be true?
options: Only the KMS key's key policy needs to allow it; IAM is irrelevant for KMS
Only the principal's IAM policy needs to allow it; the key policy is just a formality
Either the IAM policy or the key policy needs to allow it, whichever is more permissive
Both the principal's IAM policy and the KMS key's key policy need to allow it — it's an intersection, not an either/or
questions.explain: KMS access requires both layers to agree: the IAM policy attached to the user/role AND the resource-based key policy attached to the key itself. Most customer-managed keys ship with a default key policy that delegates control back to IAM, which is why many engineers never notice this layer.

questions.q: What actually happens when a KMS customer-managed key or a Key Vault key rotates on schedule?
options: All previously encrypted data is automatically re-encrypted under the new key
New key material is generated for future encryption, while old key material/versions are retained so existing ciphertext stays decryptable
The old key is deleted immediately, making old ciphertext permanently unreadable
Rotation only changes the key's display name, not its cryptographic material
questions.explain: Rotation is not the same as re-encryption. Both Key Vault and KMS generate new material for new encryption operations going forward, while retaining old key versions/material so data encrypted previously remains decryptable.

questions.q: How is an application on AWS supposed to retrieve a secret at runtime without hardcoding it?
options: By storing the secret in a plaintext environment variable checked into source control
By emailing the secret to the application's maintainer each time it changes
The compute resource (EC2, Lambda, ECS task) is given an IAM role, and the application calls Secrets Manager or KMS using that role's temporary credentials
By disabling IAM entirely so any request to Secrets Manager succeeds
questions.explain: The pattern is the same shape on both clouds: the compute identity (IAM role on AWS, managed identity on Azure) is granted permission to the secret store, and the application authenticates as itself at runtime instead of embedding the secret anywhere.
